set.tovw: Two tellings 1936/1949 of one legend; landing real (1880 history), gold unproven; nothing found

tw-mi-agards-landing-gold.st: The 1936 telling (WPA river-straightening engineer Dana P. Smith) calls him Jean Agard, French trader, with a house a mile N of the village; his two daughters never knew where the gold was, and a century of spasmodic searches and a medium's directions found nothing.

set.pl: Boston crossing, Mineral Range RR between Hancock and Calumet (Pinkerton 1907); pin at Boston Location
set.st: 15 Sep 1893, 9:30 a.m.: four masked men held up the Mineral Range train 'at a crossing in the woods, called Boston' between Hancock and Calumet and took the $70,000 Calumet & Hecla payroll (the press said $75,000). The robbers (Butler, King, La Liberty and the Hogans) hid the money in La Liberty's depot trunk; it was stolen from the trunk by the Marquette night depot master and a livery keeper (Shoupe and Winters), who buried it in the ground four miles north of Marquette. After La Liberty's confession Deputy Foley got them to reveal it, and Pinkerton recovered $69,935; $65 was missing. Both hiding places were emptied in 1893.
set.t: RECOVERED 1893 (all but $65). Look-only history marker; railroad grade.
pinev: Pinkerton 1907 names the 'Boston' woods crossing between Hancock and Calumet; pin at Boston Location, r1500 (crossing not fixed)

src: L'Anse Sentinel, 7 Oct 1893, p. 1 'The Money Recovered' (Newspapers.com 613759905)

set.st: Bogus Island, once ringed by water in the Portage River marsh of Jackson County, by the Michigan Central RR at Leoni, was the 1849 base of a gang of counterfeiters who made bogus coin in a cave by a knoll in the centre until federal agents took 8-10 of them. In 1933 the Jackson paper placed it in the swamp near Leoni where an air-mail plane crashed; the cave was later filled in. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself.

tw-mi-bogus-island-counterfeiters.st: The 1933 story: pilot Harold L. Neff crashed in the swamp owned by Frank King, Vern Chappel and Jim Bates; the cave, reached by boat, was still there when King bought part about 1903 and was later filled in; the gang had dynamited the MC tracks in Leoni village, and one member escaped to California, came back rich, and had the charges dropped.
src: Jackson Citizen Patriot, 19 Sep 1933, p. 1 (Newspapers.com 1163176384), cont. p. 2 (1163176386)

set.tovw: One wire 1902; local paper silent; no find
set.st: Andrew Jackson of Niles hid a couple of thousand dollars in gold after a local bank failed; a stroke took his speech and he died without telling where. His children planned to search. He died on 25 Jun 1902; a probate notice followed in July. The local paper called him perhaps the wealthiest Black resident of Berrien County; he ran a carrying business, owned several lots and had a habit of hiding his money. He was said to have tried to tell where he had buried gold coin before the stroke took his speech. His estate (Dec 1902) was about $1,600, including $800 in cash, most likely his bank deposit; no hidden gold was reported found. Pin is the street corner of his home, not the spot itself. The Niles Daily Star printed only his funeral notice (Second Baptist); no find reported.
pinev: 1904 directory: Andrew Jackson, 399 N. 8th St, just N of Ferry St (he died 1902; the entry may be a son). Pin at the Ferry/Eighth corner; street maps were not reachable to shift it the few metres N.
